notes.summary: A syllogism gives two or three statements about groups (cats, dogs, pens) and asks which conclusions must follow. Treat every statement as true even if it sounds silly. Draw the smallest Venn diagram the statements allow, then test each conclusion. A definite conclusion must hold in every possible diagram; a possibility conclusion needs only one diagram where it can happen.

concepts.title: The four statement types
concepts.body:
Every statement is one of four kinds. Learn the picture for each:
StatementPictureWhat it really says
All A are BA circle fully inside BEvery A is a B. B may have more members.
Some A are BA and B overlapAt least one A is a B. It may even be all of them.
No A is BA and B apartNot even one A is a B.
Some A are not BPart of A (marked ×) outside BAt least one A is outside B.

"Some" means "at least one". It never means "only some", so "Some A are B" does not tell you that some A are not B.

concepts.title: Words that mean the same thing
concepts.body:
• All: every, each, any, all of them.
  • Some: a few, many, most, several, at least one, a lot of.
  • No: none, not a single, not any, never. In SSC papers "All A are not B" is read as "No A is B".
  • Only A are B means "All B are A". Example: "Only doctors are surgeons" means every surgeon is a doctor.
  • Only a few A are B means two things together: some A are B, and some A are not B.
Rewrite every statement in one of the four standard forms before you draw anything.

concepts.title: The Venn diagram method
concepts.body:
1. Draw the first statement as its basic picture.
  2. Add the second statement using the group the two statements share (the middle term).
  3. Draw only what is stated. If nothing links two groups, keep them unlinked in your mind: they may or may not meet.
  4. Test each conclusion. If you can draw any valid diagram where it is false, it does not follow.

Mini example: All cats are dogs. Some dogs are pets. The figure shows the smallest diagram. "Some cats are pets" does not follow, because pets can touch the dogs circle without touching cats. "Some dogs are cats" does follow, because the cats circle sits inside dogs.

concepts.title: What one statement gives you
concepts.body:
From a single statement you can turn it around (convert it) only in these ways:
StatementFollowsDoes not follow
All A are BSome A are B, Some B are AAll B are A
Some A are BSome B are AAll A are B, Some A are not B
No A is BNo B is A, Some A are not B, Some B are not AAnything with "Some A are B"
Some A are not BNothing newSome B are not A, Some A are B

concepts.title: Joining two statements: the quick table
concepts.body:
Line the statements up so the shared group is in the middle: "A–B" then "B–C". Then read the A–C result:
First (A–B)Second (B–C)Conclusion
AllAllAll A are C
AllNoNo A is C
SomeAllSome A are C
SomeNoSome A are not C
NoAllSome C are not A (read it backwards)
NoSomeSome C are not A
AllSomeNo definite A–C link
SomeSomeNo definite A–C link
NoNoNo definite A–C link

If the shared group is not in the middle, first convert a statement (for example "Some B are A" becomes "Some A are B"). "All" cannot be turned around fully, so only use this when the table still fits.

concepts.title: Possibility conclusions
concepts.body:
A conclusion like "Some A being C is a possibility" asks: can I draw at least one valid diagram where it is true?
  • It follows if no statement forbids it. Unlinked groups can always possibly meet, and one group can possibly be fully inside another.
  • It fails if a statement blocks it. "No A is B" makes "Some A being B" impossible. "All A are B" makes "Some A being not B" impossible.
  • Anything that is definitely true is also possible.

Mini example: All roses are flowers. Some flowers are red. "All red things being roses is a possibility" follows: the red circle can sit inside roses and the statements still hold.

concepts.title: Either–or conclusions
concepts.body:
Sometimes neither conclusion follows alone, but one of the two must be true. Mark "Either I or II follows" only when all three checks pass:
  1. Both conclusions talk about the same two groups.
  2. Neither follows by itself.
  3. They form a pair that covers every case: "Some A are B" with "No A is B", or "All A are B" with "Some A are not B".

Example: Some flowers are red. Some red things are roses. I: Some flowers are roses. II: No rose is a flower. Neither is certain, but one of them has to be true, so either I or II follows.

concepts.title: Three statements
concepts.body: Work in a chain. Join statements 1 and 2, then 2 and 3, and draw all the groups in one diagram. For a conclusion that skips a group (A–D, say), check whether the links between them are all definite. One broken link (an All–Some or Some–Some join) means no definite conclusion, though a possibility conclusion may still follow.

varieties.name: Two statements, definite conclusions
varieties.how: Draw both statements in one diagram. A conclusion follows only if it is true in every diagram you can draw.

example.q:
Statements: All pens are books. Some books are bags.
Conclusions: I. Some pens are bags. II. Some bags are books.
steps: Draw pens inside books. Draw bags overlapping books.
Bags need not touch the pens part, so I does not follow (All + Some gives no definite link).
"Some books are bags" turned around is "Some bags are books", so II follows.

varieties.name: Three or more statements
varieties.how: Join the statements in pairs with the quick table, then test each conclusion in a single diagram.

example.q:
Statements: Some cups are plates. All plates are bowls. No bowl is a spoon.
Conclusions: I. Some cups are bowls. II. No plate is a spoon. III. Some cups are spoons.
steps: Some cups are plates + All plates are bowls: Some + All gives "Some cups are bowls". I follows.
All plates are bowls + No bowl is a spoon: All + No gives "No plate is a spoon". II follows.
Some cups are bowls + No bowl is a spoon gives only "Some cups are not spoons". III is not certain.
example.answer: Only conclusions I and II follow

varieties.name: Possibility conclusions
varieties.how: Ask "can I draw it?" A possibility follows unless a No or All statement blocks it.

example.q:
Statements: All roses are flowers. Some flowers are red.
Conclusions: I. All red things being roses is a possibility. II. Some roses being not flowers is a possibility.
steps: Red only has to overlap flowers. Nothing stops the whole red circle from sitting inside roses, so I is possible.
"All roses are flowers" puts every rose inside flowers, so a rose outside flowers is impossible. II fails.

varieties.name: One statement, inferences
varieties.how: Use the one-statement table: All gives Some both ways, Some turns around, No turns around, Some-not gives nothing new.

example.q:
Statement: All painters are artists.
Conclusions: I. Some artists are painters. II. All artists are painters.
steps: All painters are artists, so the painters circle sits inside artists.
The painters part of artists exists, so "Some artists are painters" follows.
Artists may include people who are not painters, so II does not follow.

tips: Rewrite each statement in a standard form (All, Some, No, Some not) before drawing.
Draw the smallest diagram first, then try to break each conclusion with another valid diagram.
Learn the quick table: All + All = All, All + No = No, Some + All = Some, Some + No = Some not.
All + Some, Some + Some and No + No never give a definite link between the end groups.
Whatever is definitely true is also a possibility.
For either–or, check the same two groups, neither follows alone, and a Some/No or All/Some-not pair.
With three statements, check each conclusion against the chain of links; one weak link breaks a definite conclusion.
traps: "All A are B" does not give "All B are A"; it gives only "Some B are A".
"Some A are not B" cannot be turned around into "Some B are not A".
Real-world knowledge does not count. If the statements say all fish can fly, they can.
A conclusion that is only possible must not be marked as definite, and the other way round.
Do not mark either–or when one of the two conclusions already follows by itself.

questions.q:
Statements:
All cats are dogs.
All dogs are animals.
Conclusions:
I. All cats are animals.
II. Some animals are cats.
options: Only conclusion I follows
Only conclusion II follows
Both conclusions I and II follow
Neither conclusion I nor II follows
questions.solution:
Cats ⊂ Dogs ⊂ Animals.
I: every cat is inside Animals ✓.
II: since all cats are animals, some animals are cats ✓.
Both follow.

questions.q:
Statements:
All pens are books.
No book is a table.
Conclusions:
I. No pen is a table.
II. Some tables are pens.
options: Only conclusion I follows
Only conclusion II follows
Both conclusions I and II follow
Neither conclusion I nor II follows
questions.solution:
Pens lie inside Books, and Books do not touch Tables.
So Pens cannot touch Tables: I follows.
II says some tables are pens, which is impossible.
Only I follows.

questions.q:
Statements:
Some boys are players.
All players are tall.
Conclusions:
I. Some boys are tall.
II. All tall persons are boys.
options: Only conclusion I follows
Only conclusion II follows
Both conclusions I and II follow
Neither conclusion I nor II follows
questions.solution:
The boys who are players are inside Players, and all players are tall.
So some boys are tall: I follows.
Tall persons may include non-boys: II does not follow.
Only I follows.

questions.q:
Statements:
Some flowers are red.
Some red things are roses.
Conclusions:
I. Some flowers are roses.
II. No rose is a flower.
options: Only conclusion I follows
Only conclusion II follows
Either conclusion I or II follows
Neither conclusion I nor II follows
questions.solution:
Two "Some" statements give no definite link between Flowers and Roses, so neither I nor II follows alone.
But I ("Some") and II ("No") are about the same two groups and one of them must be true.
So either I or II follows.

questions.q:
Statements:
All teachers are doctors.
Some doctors are engineers.
Conclusions:
I. Some teachers being engineers is a possibility.
II. All engineers being teachers is a possibility.
options: Only conclusion I follows
Only conclusion II follows
Both conclusions I and II follow
Neither conclusion I nor II follows
questions.solution:
Teachers ⊂ Doctors; Engineers overlap Doctors.
I: we can draw Engineers overlapping Teachers ✓ possible.
II: we can draw Engineers fully inside Teachers (still inside Doctors, so "some doctors are engineers" stays true) ✓ possible.
Both follow.

questions.q:
Statements:
No apple is a mango.
All mangoes are fruits.
Some fruits are bananas.
Conclusions:
I. Some fruits are not apples.
II. Some mangoes being apples is a possibility.
options: Only conclusion I follows
Only conclusion II follows
Both conclusions I and II follow
Neither conclusion I nor II follows
questions.solution:
All mangoes are fruits, and no mango is an apple.
So the mangoes are fruits that are not apples: I follows.
II is impossible because "No apple is a mango" forbids any overlap.
Only I follows.

flashcards.front: "All A are B" gives which definite conclusion?
flashcards.back: Some B are A (not "All B are A")
No definite conclusion between the end groups
Same two groups, neither follows alone, and they are a Some/No or All/Some-not pair
